toc.title: Burnt out on digging up the past
You wouldn't ask a non-lifter to lift 500 pounds
Ask about now, not back then
What this looks like in a session

blocks.p: Stop trying to force yourself to revisit the most painful moments of your life before you have the skills and the capacity to handle them. At least, that's what I think. You can do what you want, but that's my recommendation. I think true transformation happens when we prioritize stability over the agonizing search for why. Building a balanced internal foundation is the missing prerequisite for lasting emotional freedom.

blocks.h: Burnt out on digging up the past

blocks.p: People come to me, as therapy clients, coaching clients, and students, because they need something different. They are rightfully burnt out by years and years of talk therapy that focuses on digging up past memories and attempting to process them: replaying them in their mind, sitting with all the agonizing pain of it all, or telling the story over and over again, whether their eyes are moving back and forth or not, whether the therapist is holding a wand or not.
I can see why they're burning out. This is too much, but it's not uncommon in therapy in 2026.

For many people, simply going to therapy and talking with a caring other is enough to help them move out of whatever stuckness they're in. They don't need to go into the details of the past. They just need someone to listen, maybe hold them accountable, and come up with and do some homework together. Fairly simple, and the risk of dysregulation is very low.

Some people do need to, or want to, confront the details of their past, and they're ready to. They share the details with a caring therapist, maybe they cry it out, and they move on with life. Again, the risk of dysregulation is fairly low. This person can handle it.

For others, though, confronting the past is not what they need. Focusing on the pains of the past does not bring a cathartic cry. It might bring panic or rage, or numb them to the experience of the present moment. It might look like they're telling their trauma story and confronting their pains, but really they've checked out. They're in the room, but emotionally, they're not.
These are very different therapy clients: the people who need to talk it out and are ready to, and the people who are probably worse off if they start talking about the past before they're ready.

blocks.h: You wouldn't ask a non-lifter to lift 500 pounds

blocks.p: "Well, Justin, they're just weak and they need to deal with it."
I humbly suggest that you are in no position to gauge someone else's self-development. But thank you so much anyway.
Would you expect someone who doesn't go to the gym to lift 500 pounds? Of course not. Telling that person to deal with it would subject them to potentially very bad results. That's pretty obvious.

The same applies to emotional regulation. Emotions are not just chemicals in the brain, or free-floating experiences that somehow live within us. They are directly connected to the state of our body. Our body's state can change over time and allow more emotional capacity, just like muscles can grow over time and allow you to lift heavier things.

So it would make no sense to ask someone who avoids their emotions to now pay attention to the most difficult ones, just like it would make no sense to ask a non-bodybuilder to lift 500 pounds. That would be flooding, and it obviously sounds like a bad idea. Their body does not have the capacity for it. For now, at least.

So when they go into a therapy session and tell the most horrific instances of their life, they are being flooded, even if they're moving their eyes back and forth, even if they're telling their story over and over again to desensitize themselves to it, even if they're sitting with their typical compulsion and withholding the impulse to perform it.

I have heard from so many clients that these techniques simply made things worse for them. For all clients? Of course not. I'm specifically talking about those who do not have the capacity to confront the most difficult pieces of their life. When people with little distress tolerance confront their pains, they end up retraumatized. They end up solidifying their deepest shames and guilts and panics and rages, and are overwhelmed even further.

So getting unstuck is not going to happen through a historical investigation of the past, and definitely not from flooding the system with the details of the past. And not by rehashing what happened this past week, with no purpose, week after week after week.
We need to do something different. We need a physiological shift in the present moment. We need to build capacity, and gradually confront difficult topics if and when that person is ready.

"No, seriously, Justin. They just need to get over it." Or maybe you're saying it about yourself: "I need to just get over it." If it were that easy, sure. But if it were that easy, you wouldn't be searching for ways to get unstuck. It's not simply a choice, which I'm sure you're aware of.
This comes down to how our nervous system fundamentally operates. Survival always trumps logic, and even willpower.

Your nervous system is not a rational debating club, or something you can just choose to overcome. It's a biological mechanism that's been honed over millions of years of evolution. It's been around well before us humans, and it operated within every species well before our consciousness. It's biological.

It operates largely outside of our awareness and outside of our direct control. If it's in a dysregulated state, it's not because you've chosen it. It's probably a normal, expected result of your life context, maybe for a very, very long time.

When you're dealing with a system that's been chronically dysregulated, it doesn't care about your therapy goals, or your intellectual desire to process something or confront it or sit with it. It cares about one thing: keeping you alive. To come out of this chronic survival state, the body needs more ventral vagal parasympathetic activation. You don't have to worry about the words, but that's the biology that supports your capacity to think critically, to be in stillness, to play with others, and to connect socially. It's kind of important.

People who do not benefit from processing the past likely have a low level of this safety state present. Maybe they have way too much flight or fight, or they're collapsed and shut down, or they exist in a panicky freeze. Regardless, they are always in a defensive state, or easily triggered into one by specific contextual cues that evoke painful past moments that are relived in the body.

So when they attempt to heal by confronting their painful past, their body is not in a regulated state to contain and process what comes up. Trying to excavate deep traumatic memories when your system is already overwhelmed is like trying to repair a car's engine while driving at top speed through a storm. It's not just inefficient, it's dangerous, and kind of dumb.

So let's be crystal clear here. Establishing a baseline of physical, environmental, and interpersonal safety is non-negotiable. It's the first step. It's not optional. We have to have literal safety. This isn't just nice to have. It's fundamental. We need safe people and safe environments.
Attempting any kind of self-development without these pieces is probably not going to go very well. We don't need perfection, but we need safe enough.

blocks.h: Ask about now, not back then

blocks.p: So what do we do about all this? I recommend doing less asking, "What happened to me back then?" and more asking, "How does my body feel right now?" More connection to the present moment, in very simple ways.

Questions like: How does my body feel right now? How am I breathing? What do I hear around me? What's my skin touching? These present-moment questions help us focus on the here and now. And once we're in the here and now, then we can address discomfort, if we want to.

blocks.h: What this looks like in a session

blocks.p: Here's an example. Just yesterday, as of recording this, I did a session with someone who typically has lots and lots of anxiety and hypervigilance.

It was our second session, and they came in at a five out of 10 on their anxiety scale. I did a very simple present-moment thing with them. I asked about their breath and what they hear. Very simple. They dropped from a five to a three just from that. The three felt like calm to them, with some fidgetiness. They were leaning forward with their hands clasped.

Since they were now in a regulated state, I asked if they were up for a little exercise to challenge their safety state. They said, yeah, sure, they were up for whatever. If I had asked when they were at a seven out of 10, it would probably have been a no. We venture into potential discomfort from a regulated state, like a three out of 10.

So I said something I knew would trigger a little anxiety: someone's name that was relevant to them. And I was right. It brought them to a six out of 10. We permitted the six out of 10 to be there without rejecting it. We just paid attention to it, and then shifted our focus to the breath and the external sounds. Soon the client said they were back down to a three.

We did this really simple process, with the same trigger from me, a couple more times. Each time, the reaction went down a little, from six to five to four, to eventually not at all. They just weren't triggered by it anymore.
Then, with their permission, I gave them another name that I knew would trigger them, and it again brought them quickly to a six out of 10. But by now, their body already knew how to recover.

I didn't ask the client to tell me about these people or share past incidents. In fact, when they started to tell me, I said of course they could, but let's also focus on the way their body was breathing and the sounds around them. At that point, they didn't need to narratively process. They could leave the cognitive processing and focus on the somatic, on the body, on that six out of 10.

They were even able to identify where that six out of 10 showed up in their body, which was in their calves. They identified which calf, and what their leg wanted to do in response to the slight triggers. They wanted to get up and leave, which makes sense. Did they want to get up and leave because I'm a jerk who kept triggering them? That's a potential narrative, and I hope that's not the case. But really, their body was responding to the trigger with flight activation. When you have anxiety, that's more flight activation.

All of this happens in the present moment: noticing the intensity of the anxiety, noticing the tension in the calves and the impulse to get up, noticing the breath and the sounds around us. It's all very present moment.

Prioritizing the present is not dismissing, rejecting, or stuffing down the past. This isn't avoidance. Prioritizing the present is building capacity at a biological level, just like putting the reps in at the gym builds muscle.

We can use this new foundation to process more difficult things later on in therapy, if a client wants to. And we won't need to move our eyes back and forth, or use a wand, or sit with it, or tell the story over, or whatever else. We simply exist in the present moment and whatever it brings. This sounds different because it is different. That's what people keep telling me, at least.

The old models of therapy, and self-help too, focused on uncovering the subconscious, or training behavior, or changing your thinking, or sitting through reliving the most painful moments of your life. I don't think any of this cuts it anymore, at least for those in the most desperate need of change. Some people are ready for that and can handle it. That's fine, but that's not who I'm talking about.

The new model I hope you'll consider is to strengthen nervous system capacity by gradually connecting with discomfort while regulated. If you can do this, then you can pay attention to your subconscious, or process the past, or change behavior, or think differently, or whatever. All of that becomes way easier, because you're regulated now, and the more regulated you are, the easier those things become.

This is possible not through force. That's not the way it works. Not through flooding, but through patient, consistent micro-regulation practices that connect you to the present, and through understanding that the way you are makes sense in the context of your life.
This is how we get unstuck. Not by digging up the past, but by building a present capable of holding anything. And the past, if you want to process it, that's fine too.
Let's wrap this up by pausing here and just noticing our breath.
Just real quick. Don't control it. How is your body naturally breathing already? If it changes on its own because you've paid attention, that's fine, but don't control it. Just notice it.
As you notice, maybe the next breath that comes in: is it into your chest or your belly? Is it more full or more shallow? On the next one, and on the next one: is it more tense or relaxed?
On the next natural breath, notice what you hear around you. Maybe in your space, or outside of your space. What else do you hear?
Stay here for a few more breaths, and just focus on your natural breathing.
All right. Great job. You can do this more than once a day, right?
